00:05:27.000 --> 00:05:42.000
Randy Harlow: Depending on the project and depending on both the contractors and the owners that are involved there, the level of sophistication varies, but your hypothesis that there's not one.

00:05:43.000 --> 00:05:49.000
Randy Harlow: established way of doing it is absolutely correct.

00:05:48.000 --> 00:05:49.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:05:49.000 --> 00:05:52.000
Randy Harlow: There are various…

00:05:52.000 --> 00:06:02.000
Randy Harlow: groups that have tried to standardize it over the years. The American Institute of Architects is a big one, um, that have tried to say, this is how RFIs should be.

00:06:02.000 --> 00:06:11.000
Randy Harlow: uh, processed and dealt with. Um, but they… none of… no one way has kind of taken the… taken the…

00:06:11.000 --> 00:06:14.000
Micah Santos: Mm-hmm.

00:06:12.000 --> 00:06:16.000
Randy Harlow: Long term strength or I guess has been come out on top yet.

00:06:16.000 --> 00:06:22.000
Micah Santos: Okay. Could you give us some insight as to maybe why that could be?

00:06:21.000 --> 00:06:31.000
Randy Harlow: Uh, the sophistication level of the owners in particular, like, sometimes you'll have just a… a home builder. Uh, someone is…

00:06:31.000 --> 00:06:48.000
Randy Harlow: Building their own house and, and you compare that with, um, a mega project, something like Sound Transit does of building light rail for eight miles, right? So there, there's just a wide range of, of dollar values of these contracts in that.

00:06:39.000 --> 00:06:40.000
Micah Santos: Mm-hmm.

00:06:48.000 --> 00:06:59.000
Randy Harlow: leads to how much can go into administering them, and how much is available for that. So, cost plays a huge part, and then the level of.

00:06:59.000 --> 00:07:07.000
Randy Harlow: the contracting entities involved. So if, for example, you're able to say this is the best way to go, and it's.

00:07:07.000 --> 00:07:23.000
Randy Harlow: really easy for everybody to implement, that's gonna have a opportunity to kind of catch the market. Uh, whereas if it's one more way of doing things that some people do on spreadsheets and other people do on.

00:07:23.000 --> 00:07:31.000
Randy Harlow: specialized construction management software. And at that point, it might get a little dicier.

00:07:31.000 --> 00:07:36.000
Micah Santos: I see, I see, okay. Um, next…

00:07:38.000 --> 00:07:48.000
Micah Santos: I guess for Sound Transit specifically because we're trying to use data about the expansion into the light rail expansion into Bellevue and Redmond.

00:07:48.000 --> 00:07:54.000
Micah Santos: How are RFIs prioritized by you all during the project? Or how were they, I guess?

00:07:54.000 --> 00:07:59.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, it's a good question.

00:07:59.000 --> 00:08:10.000
Randy Harlow: The project that you're talking about, the Eastlink extension, all the way across, is comprised of roughly 12 different construction contracts.

00:08:10.000 --> 00:08:25.000
Randy Harlow: So, each contract and contractor has their own way of doing it, and there's different contracting methodologies involved there, too, that come into play. For the most part, um, the…

00:08:25.000 --> 00:08:32.000
Randy Harlow: The only categorization that's used is the consistent document control program of SharePoint.

00:08:32.000 --> 00:08:48.000
Randy Harlow: Um, but as far as prioritization, most of that prioritization happens with the contractor indicating a date that they need the response by, and then that date usually is the one that.

00:08:48.000 --> 00:09:01.000
Randy Harlow: the owner uses to try and prioritize which answers are needed most quickly. Um, it's not always, uh, like a first-in, first-out kind of approach. Uh, it's much more a…

00:08:59.000 --> 00:09:00.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:09:01.000 --> 00:09:12.000
Randy Harlow: if a contractor says, I need this by X date in order to not be delayed or not have more costs, that's what kind of takes the priority.

00:09:12.000 --> 00:09:17.000
Micah Santos: I see, so it's very… based on, sort of, due date.

00:09:17.000 --> 00:09:33.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, yeah, for the most part, there's a lot, there's a lot of differences in RFIs between how complex they are and easy to answer. Um, so some of those require a bit more time. Some contractors understand that and will say, I need it within two weeks.

00:09:17.000 --> 00:09:19.000
Micah Santos: So they speak.

00:09:25.000 --> 00:09:26.000
Micah Santos: Mmhm.

00:09:33.000 --> 00:09:44.000
Randy Harlow: understanding that it's a long one. Others will say I need it tomorrow just because they want to say, Oh, I I need it as fast as I can get it. there is some.

00:09:42.000 --> 00:09:43.000
Micah Santos: Ah, okay.

00:09:44.000 --> 00:09:48.000
Randy Harlow: human factor plugged in there.

00:09:48.000 --> 00:09:49.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:09:49.000 --> 00:09:51.000
Micah Santos: Sort of.

00:09:51.000 --> 00:09:57.000
Micah Santos: On the topic of that, like, complexity, when an RFI has missing data.

00:09:57.000 --> 00:10:09.000
Micah Santos: or is just otherwise messy? How do y'all deal with that? Do you just… do you have to send in, like, another RFI for that contractor that gave you the RFI? Okay, tell us more about this, or, like, do you just leave it?

00:10:08.000 --> 00:10:25.000
Randy Harlow: There's a couple of ways of handling it. The easiest way for it to actually get resolved is for the responder to pick up the phone and call the person that asked the question and actually have a conversation saying, I need some additional information to be able to answer this.

00:10:25.000 --> 00:10:27.000
Micah Santos: Okay, okay.

00:10:27.000 --> 00:10:38.000
Randy Harlow: In the absence of being able to do that, a lot of it turns into a back and forth of there's not enough information in this RFI. That's the answer to the RFI.

00:10:37.000 --> 00:10:38.000
Micah Santos: Thanks.

00:10:38.000 --> 00:10:47.000
Randy Harlow: And then another RFI gets written. Here's more information that I need more information. So it can bounce back and forth like that as well.

00:10:47.000 --> 00:10:52.000
Micah Santos: I see, okay. But, at the end of the day, you all make sure you have the information you need.

00:10:52.000 --> 00:10:56.000
Micah Santos: Before you make any judgments about how important the RFI is.

00:10:58.000 --> 00:11:01.000
Randy Harlow: Uh, usually we'll try and…

00:11:01.000 --> 00:11:09.000
Randy Harlow: Understand the topic and where it fits into the project's cost and schedule, and…

00:11:09.000 --> 00:11:12.000
Randy Harlow: Even without all the information.

00:11:12.000 --> 00:11:19.000
Randy Harlow: necessary to answer it, you can get a good idea of how important a particular RFI is.

00:11:19.000 --> 00:11:23.000
Randy Harlow: Obviously, that's a judgment call.

00:11:23.000 --> 00:11:31.000
Randy Harlow: Sometimes things slip through the cracks that are very important and vice versa. A lot of attention is paid to.

00:11:31.000 --> 00:11:33.000
Randy Harlow: very unimportant.

00:11:33.000 --> 00:11:35.000
Randy Harlow: Rfis.

Sandra: Let's go! So…

00:22:36.000 --> 00:22:37.000
Randy Harlow: Thank you.

00:22:38.000 --> 00:22:41.000
Micah Santos: Um, it's been 20 minutes.

00:22:39.000 --> 00:22:40.000
Sandra: Yeah, okay.

00:22:41.000 --> 00:22:48.000
Micah Santos: We… I have a couple more general questions I'd like to ask if you have time, but if not…

00:22:47.000 --> 00:22:48.000
Randy Harlow: Okay.

00:22:48.000 --> 00:22:50.000
Micah Santos: Thanks. Okay. Perfect.

00:22:48.000 --> 00:22:52.000
Randy Harlow: Yep. I've got till the bottom of the hour, so sure.

00:22:51.000 --> 00:22:53.000
Micah Santos: Nice.

00:22:53.000 --> 00:22:55.000
Micah Santos: So…

00:23:04.000 --> 00:23:06.000
Micah Santos: One second.

00:23:10.000 --> 00:23:13.000
Micah Santos: Um, for Sound Transit, the project, um.

00:23:13.000 --> 00:23:19.000
Micah Santos: East expansion specifically, were there any specific or new problems that had to be addressed that.

00:23:19.000 --> 00:23:23.000
Micah Santos: are sort of untraditional, in a sense. Like, I heard about…

00:23:23.000 --> 00:23:28.000
Micah Santos: Like electricity killing fish in Lake Washington.

00:23:28.000 --> 00:23:52.000
Randy Harlow: That's a rather new one. But yeah, the whole concept of running light rail across a floating bridge was a problem that the project had to tackle. The issue that you're speaking of there with the electricity in Lake Washington, that's intended to prevent the degradation of the bridge itself.

00:23:28.000 --> 00:23:30.000
Micah Santos: Yeah, anything like that.

00:23:52.000 --> 00:23:58.000
Randy Harlow: And so there's a cathodic protection system that is running to…

00:23:58.000 --> 00:24:05.000
Randy Harlow: basically inject current into the bridge so that the reinforcing steel doesn't rust prematurely.

00:24:04.000 --> 00:24:06.000
Micah Santos: I see, okay.

00:24:05.000 --> 00:24:15.000
Randy Harlow: And it sounds like a few of those cables are a bit too long, and they're hitting the bottom of the lake.

00:24:15.000 --> 00:24:16.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:24:15.000 --> 00:24:31.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, that we are still investigating to see if there's something more to it. But that was one of the the going across the floating bridge itself was the big thing that had to get tackled for Eastlink. It took a very unique.

00:24:31.000 --> 00:24:39.000
Randy Harlow: system to be able to adapt the tracks as the water level changes, because.

00:24:39.000 --> 00:24:48.000
Randy Harlow: Trains don't really like having things vary as far as the elevation of the tracks from one point to another.

00:24:47.000 --> 00:24:53.000
Micah Santos: I see. How long did it take for that all to be sort of.

00:24:53.000 --> 00:24:54.000
Micah Santos: And.

00:24:54.000 --> 00:24:57.000
Micah Santos: solved, I guess.

00:24:55.000 --> 00:25:06.000
Randy Harlow: That's all. Between design and construction, I think the Eastlink program was working on that issue for roughly 15 years.

00:25:06.000 --> 00:25:07.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:25:07.000 --> 00:25:08.000
Randy Harlow: So…

00:25:10.000 --> 00:25:14.000
Micah Santos: Quite a long time. I if I'm not mistaken, I think the bidding.

00:25:14.000 --> 00:25:20.000
Micah Santos: for some of the sections was 15 or so years ago, am I correct?

00:25:20.000 --> 00:25:22.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, it's been a while.

00:25:22.000 --> 00:25:23.000
Micah Santos: Okay.

00:25:23.000 --> 00:25:29.000
Micah Santos: This is a little bit off-topic of RFIs, but how was the bidding process for everything? How did that go?

00:25:29.000 --> 00:25:45.000
Randy Harlow: It was a lengthy process because the agency chose different contracting styles across between Seattle and Redmond. So you've got some traditional design bid build, some.

00:25:45.000 --> 00:25:55.000
Randy Harlow: design-build approaches, and then a few general contractor construction manager GCCM approaches. Um, and so that…

00:25:53.000 --> 00:25:54.000
Micah Santos: Yes.

00:25:55.000 --> 00:26:02.000
Randy Harlow: Each of those has its own nuances as far as bidding and contracting, and so…

00:26:02.000 --> 00:26:07.000
Randy Harlow: The bid kind of procurement process was probably a good…

00:26:07.000 --> 00:26:11.000
Randy Harlow: three or four of those years in the making.

00:26:11.000 --> 00:26:13.000
Micah Santos: Okay, okay.

00:26:13.000 --> 00:26:29.000
Micah Santos: And a little bit just to educate ourselves, I think, about the differences between like GCs, design teams and all that. Do you think you could sort of give us an overview of what that looks like? I think we understand generally the difference between subcontractor and general contractor.

00:26:30.000 --> 00:26:35.000
Micah Santos: We don't know much about the other teams, if there are ones involved.

00:26:35.000 --> 00:26:53.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, so Sound Transit is the owner, and there's a team of staff assigned to each project to help manage that contract with the general contractor. There's also a design team that's hired independently for.

00:26:53.000 --> 00:26:54.000
Randy Harlow: Some of those…

00:26:54.000 --> 00:27:10.000
Randy Harlow: contracts, others, you know, depending on the situation. Um, but Sound Transit also employs a group of consultants that are hired specific for the projects, uh, called construction management consultants, and those.

00:27:10.000 --> 00:27:18.000
Randy Harlow: uh, those consultants sit in between the owner and the GC, um, basically working like an extension of staff.

00:27:18.000 --> 00:27:25.000
Randy Harlow: So those are the big groupings that show up on our projects for the most part.

00:27:24.000 --> 00:27:26.000
Micah Santos: I see.

00:27:31.000 --> 00:27:36.000
Sandra: Okay, I have a question. So other than…

00:27:36.000 --> 00:27:52.000
Sandra: the big challenge of putting a big bridge over water. What was some other like unexpected like roadblocks or speed bumps in like the process of like making that happen like stuff they didn't expect.

00:27:50.000 --> 00:27:51.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah.

00:27:53.000 --> 00:28:08.000
Randy Harlow: Stuff we didn't expect. We didn't expect kind of the permitting process to take as long as it did, both with the State Department of Transportation and mainly the City of Bellevue.

00:28:08.000 --> 00:28:15.000
Randy Harlow: We underestimated the complexity of some of the concerns there, so that wasn't…

00:28:15.000 --> 00:28:20.000
Randy Harlow: all the way expected. Um, there was some…

00:28:20.000 --> 00:28:26.000
Randy Harlow: Complexity in utilizing the, um, tunnels.

00:28:26.000 --> 00:28:28.000
Randy Harlow: Through Mount Baker.

00:28:28.000 --> 00:28:44.000
Randy Harlow: Um, that was a challenge that the team had to come up with in, in ways that involved using, uh, overhead contact rail, so a direct rail to transfer electricity to the trains instead of what you usually see, the cables.

00:28:44.000 --> 00:28:49.000
Randy Harlow: That are out across the rest of the alignment, so that… that complexity was new.

00:28:49.000 --> 00:28:58.000
Randy Harlow: Um, and the tunnel that was built in Bellevue, um, was utilized a different.

00:28:58.000 --> 00:28:59.000
Randy Harlow: No, no.

00:28:59.000 --> 00:29:13.000
Randy Harlow: utilized a method that we hadn't used before called sequential excavation. Um, instead of a big tunneling machine, it was chipped away at, basically, and shotcreted behind, uh, as the… as they went through.

00:29:13.000 --> 00:29:17.000
Randy Harlow: Um, there… there have been a lot of…

00:29:17.000 --> 00:29:28.000
Randy Harlow: I guess, sound complaints that we didn't anticipate. Some of them are because of the sensitivity of the areas that they're in.

00:29:28.000 --> 00:29:29.000
Micah Santos: Mmhm.

00:29:30.000 --> 00:29:43.000
Randy Harlow: And we do have a couple of really steep sections of track, which mean that our trains have to worry about icy conditions, especially when traveling downhill on them.

00:29:43.000 --> 00:29:48.000
Randy Harlow: But, um, that don't occur elsewhere in our extension, so are they…

00:29:48.000 --> 00:29:50.000
Randy Harlow: Are they…

00:29:50.000 --> 00:29:55.000
Randy Harlow: Never before seen? No. Are they things that are new to us? Yeah.

00:29:57.000 --> 00:30:01.000
Micah Santos: Actually, I have one more question since you were talking about.

00:30:01.000 --> 00:30:02.000
Micah Santos: Sort of like the…

00:30:03.000 --> 00:30:12.000
Micah Santos: how the trains need to be careful of icy conditions. I was wondering whose responsibility is that, and how do you guys allot responsibility?

00:30:12.000 --> 00:30:31.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah. Yeah. So the operating alignment is maintained and operated by King County Metro, their KC rail division. And they have a series of protocols and processes and policies that they follow.

00:30:31.000 --> 00:30:46.000
Randy Harlow: When certain weather conditions are hit. Icy conditions on those tracks are one of those. On the bridge itself, they'll slow down or stop trains depending on wind speed.

00:30:46.000 --> 00:30:48.000
Randy Harlow: And wave height.

00:30:48.000 --> 00:31:04.000
Randy Harlow: So there's, there's a variety of things that they, they've got checklists. Um, if there's any question, they will go put people out there to put eyes on them and look at it, um, just to make sure that it's safe because the, the worst thing we can do is.

00:31:04.000 --> 00:31:08.000
Randy Harlow: have the traveling public exposed to those kind of conditions.

00:31:08.000 --> 00:31:10.000
Micah Santos: Okay, okay.

00:31:15.000 --> 00:31:17.000
Sandra: Okay.

00:31:16.000 --> 00:31:19.000
Micah Santos: Let me look through our…

00:31:17.000 --> 00:31:27.000
Randy Harlow: I mean, I know we've just scratched the surface of a bunch of stuff of what I do, and we've just scratched the surface of a bunch of what you're doing, so, um, good luck to you. If you think I can be of…

00:31:27.000 --> 00:31:35.000
Randy Harlow: more help later on, or if there's anything that we can do to help you all out, please reach out to me.

00:31:35.000 --> 00:31:38.000
Micah Santos: Yes, thank you so much.

00:31:36.000 --> 00:31:43.000
Sandra: Thank you so much. Thank you for taking the time out of your day to help us with our project.

00:31:42.000 --> 00:31:46.000
Randy Harlow: Yeah, good luck, and let me know how it goes.

00:31:42.000 --> 00:31:45.000
Micah Santos: And thank you again for…

00:31:45.000 --> 00:31:47.000
Sandra: Alright.

00:31:45.000 --> 00:31:49.000
Micah Santos: Will do. Thank you. Have a good day.

00:31:47.000 --> 00:31:48.000
Sandra: Okay.
